title: The Ionization of Weak Acids and Weak Bases

children.text: Many acids and bases are weak; that is, they do not ionize fully in aqueous solution. A solution of a weak acid in water is a mixture of the nonionized acid, hydronium ion, and the conjugate base of the acid, with the nonionized acid present in the greatest concentration. A weak acid therefore increases the hydronium ion concentration in an aqueous solution (but not nearly as much as the same amount of a strong acid).
H, is a weak acid. When we add acetic acid to water, it ionizes to a small extent according to:

giving an equilibrium mixture with most of the acid present in the nonionized (molecular) form. Like all other equilibria, this equilibrium is dynamic: acetic acid molecules donate hydrogen ions to water molecules and form hydronium ions and acetate ions at the same rate as hydronium ions donate hydrogen ions to acetate ions to reform acetic acid molecules and water molecules. By measuring the pH of an aqueous solution of known concentration, we can tell that only a fraction of the weak acid is ionized at any moment. The remaining weak acid is present in the nonionized form.

At equilibrium, a solution of a weak base in water is a mixture of the nonionized base, the conjugate acid of the weak base, and hydroxide ion, with the nonionized base present in the greatest concentration. A weak base therefore increases the hydroxide ion concentration in an aqueous solution (but not as much as the same amount of a strong base).
